title: Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families
one_liner: A flat-fee, advocate-supervised 'estate file' service that gets a dead parent's or grandfather's land, shares and dormant accounts legally transferred, sold to the adult children who pay from Nairobi, Dallas or Dubai.
customer: Salaried urban and diaspora Kenyans aged 30-55 whose rural parents or grandparents died (or are old) with land still registered in a dead person's name. They pay from abroad or from the city. A secondary B2B payer is any SACCO, coop or bank that needs cleared successions before it releases deposits or lends against land.
problem: Most rural family land is still titled to a dead grandfather or father because nobody completed succession. The process needs a chief's letter, a death certificate, consents from every heir, gazettement, a wait before confirmation of grant, and then transmission at the land registry, which is often 1-3 years and many trips. Until it is done the land cannot be leased, mortgaged, subdivided or cleanly sold, siblings fight, and the deceased's SACCO deposits, coop shares, insurance and pension sit unclaimed. The real blocker is coordinating 8 to 20 relatives to sign, not the court.
solution: Wedge product is a 'Family Estate Map' for roughly KES 15-25k (pricing to be tested). The child sends photos of the title, IDs, death certificate and old share certificates over WhatsApp. An LLM pipeline extracts names and parcel numbers, handles the multiple-name and spelling-variant problem in Kenyan naming, builds the family tree and likely heirs, and lists the consents needed. It runs official land searches and asset-discovery letters to SACCOs, coops, insurers and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, then outputs a court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits. A home-county field agent collects the chief's letter and relatives' signatures or thumbprints, with video proof of consent. Partner advocates then file and shepherd the case at their own scale fees. Later upsells are surveyor subdivision and lease or loan readiness.
why_now: The generation that took up land in the 1960s-80s through settlement schemes and land-buying companies is dying now, so the succession backlog is peaking. Diaspora remittances are near record levels (roughly US$5bn a year), and families increasingly ask 'sort out the land' rather than 'build a house'. Digitised land records (Ardhisasa) and court e-filing reduce physical running, though their current coverage needs checking. LLMs can now read messy scanned title and ID documents and draft forms in English while chatting with clients in Swahili. I could not run live searches, so verify current UFAA agent rules, court e-filing scope for successions, and fee schedules before building.
revenue_model: Flat fee per estate file, paid by M-Pesa or card from abroad. Advocate fees are billed by the advocates themselves, so the company sells software and case management and does not split fees with non-lawyers. Asset discovery is a flat add-on fee, not a percentage cut of UFAA payouts, because UFAA discourages middlemen taking a share. B2B revenue is per cleaned member estate from SACCOs and coops. Later there is referral income from surveyors and land-backed lenders once titles are clean.
non_obvious_insight: Rural Kenya's biggest pool of unused collateral is land trapped in the name of the dead. The bottleneck is family coordination and evidence gathering, so the product is a coordination workflow sold to the sibling who has money and guilt, not a land registry or a lawyer marketplace. VCs looking at land-tech miss that the payer is the diaspora child, not the farmer.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Murang'a or Kakamega) and recruit two advocates who already do succession work. Build intake on WhatsApp Business, Airtable and an LLM extraction script. Sell 10 files at a pilot discount through your own family network, church and alumni groups, and diaspora WhatsApp and Facebook groups such as Kenyans in Texas or the UK. Publish a free 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' checker as lead-gen. Track days from intake to gazettement as the core metric.

title: Toddler Talk: Voice-Based Developmental Screening
one_liner: A phone-recorded three-minute parent-child talk sample plus automated screening workflow that helps pediatric practices catch speech and developmental delays earlier and capture reimbursement.
customer: Pediatric practices and health systems (developmental screening is billable under CPT 96110), Early Intervention programs and Medicaid managed care plans.
problem: Speech-language delay is a very common developmental issue, but screening relies on parent questionnaires with modest sensitivity, practices under-screen and Early Intervention waitlists are long. Kids are referred late.
solution: Phase 1 (no diagnostic claims) is a text-based well-visit screening workflow that increases completion and billing capture and collects consented audio. Phase 2 adds speech models that estimate vocabulary diversity, word combinations and turn-taking latency, giving clinicians a triage report. Phase 3 is a validated FDA pathway.
why_now: Speech models now handle child speech far better than before. Developmental screening is a CMS Child Core Set quality measure (from memory), so Medicaid plans pay for completion. Multimodal models make sample-based scoring feasible.
revenue_model: Per-screen fee or per-provider subscription ($200-500 a month), plus quality-improvement contracts with Medicaid plans, and later a per-report fee.
non_obvious_insight: Parents already record toddlers constantly. The bottleneck is not detection technology but screening completion and triage, so the winning move is to attach to the reimbursed screening code and Medicaid quality measures first and upgrade the signal later.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 independent pediatric practices through a developmental-behavioral pediatrician advisor. Run a 60-day free text-intake screening pilot. Capture consented audio for retrospective validation. Pitch one Medicaid plan's quality team on completion-rate lift.

title: Brewery Tank-Time for Fermentation Startups
one_liner: Rent the empty fermenters of struggling craft breweries to early-stage fermentation companies that cannot get pilot-scale capacity, with standard SOPs and insurance.
customer: Buyers: seed-to-Series-A companies making probiotics and postbiotics, lactic-acid-bacteria and yeast-based ingredients, cultured foods, kombucha-adjacent drinks and biocontrol products that need 1 to 30 kL runs. Sellers: craft breweries, cideries and distilleries with idle tanks.
problem: Pilot-scale food-grade fermentation capacity is scarce and expensive for startups. Meanwhile the Brewers Association says breweries used only about 55% of capacity in 2024, there were 481 closures against 300 openings in 2025, and US craft breweries fell to 9,344 by June 2026. Neither side knows how to contract safely, and food-safety, TTB and insurance issues block informal deals.
solution: A marketplace with a standardized brewery-as-CDMO package: BSL-1 organism screening, cleaning and changeover SOPs, food-facility registration checks, TTB premises guidance, a template contract and insurer-backed coverage. A rentable clip-on aeration and dissolved-oxygen kit extends tanks to low-aeration aerobic processes. Startups book tank-days and downstream time (centrifuge, filtration, cold room).
why_now: Craft brewing is in a third year of decline, with real estate and tank capacity stranded. Startup funding is tight, so cheap pilot capacity matters. Sensors and remote fermentation monitoring make third-party oversight feasible.
revenue_model: Startups pay $300 to $900 per tank-day; the brewery keeps about 80%, the platform takes 15% to 20%. Fees for SOP set-up, kit rental and insurance referral.
non_obvious_insight: Tanks are not the scarce input; validated protocols and biosafety trust are. Most brewery fermenters are unstirred and anaerobic, so the honest wedge is anaerobic and low-aeration products, with an aeration retrofit unlocking more later. A platform that standardizes the SOP and contract becomes the default channel.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 breweries within a few hours of Boston, the Bay Area or Denver that have idle 10-to-30-barrel fermenters. Work with a food-safety consultant to write a one-organism SOP. Approach 25 fermentation startups and run 3 paid pilot batches at $2k to $5k each.

title: 24/7 named-filer retainer for CRA reporting
one_liner: A follow-the-sun 'fractional PSIRT' that pre-registers, drills and files CRA Article 14 vulnerability reports on the ENISA portal for small connected-device makers.
customer: EU and non-EU manufacturers of connected products with roughly 5-250 staff and no 24/7 security team. Examples are smart-home, IP camera, e-bike and e-scooter electronics, EV charger, industrial IoT gateway, 3D printer and consumer robotics makers. Their CEO or head of product pays.
problem: Since 11 Sept 2026, manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, a fuller notice within 72 hours, and a final report later. This covers products already on the market, including 2019 models. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. The ENISA portal has no API at launch and needs 39 manual fields. Filers must be named individuals with EU Login and MFA. Picking the wrong coordinator CSIRT can invalidate a filing. The platform's 72-hour counter can show a compliant filing as overdue. Emailing a national CSIRT does not count. Small makers have no one awake on a Sunday who knows any of this.
solution: Sell a monthly retainer with four parts. (1) A pre-flight setup: named EU Login accounts, a documented coordinator-CSIRT choice, a product-to-Member-State map and the required vulnerability contact. (2) A one-page intake form and an 'awareness decision log' that keeps independent 24h/72h/14-day clocks and a defensible record of when the manufacturer became aware. (3) A rotating on-call engineer, holding one of the up-to-20 secondary filer seats under the manufacturer's written designation, who drafts and pastes the 39-field early warning within hours. (4) Twice-yearly tabletop drills that produce an audit-ready evidence file. The manufacturer stays legally responsible. We supply speed and process, not scanners.
why_now: Article 14 became binding on 11 Sept 2026 and the single reporting platform went live the same day. Registration guidance only started rolling out on 31 July. No CRA harmonised standard was in the Official Journal as of late August, and notified-body capacity is a 'best-efforts' December 2026 target. Small makers therefore have no standards shortcut and must run the reporting process by hand.
revenue_model: Setup fee of EUR 1,000-1,500. Retainer of EUR 250-600 per month by product count. Incident filing package of EUR 2-4k per event. Drill add-on of EUR 800. Later, referral or bundle deals with cyber insurers, notified-body consultants and contract manufacturers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a named human with a valid account, awake at 3am, making the 'awareness' judgment call. Scanner vendors are everywhere, but nobody sells the person and the drill. Evidence: the ENISA portal guide says 'Automate the preparation, not the filing' and lists no API, 39 fields, named-person accounts, the wrong-CSIRT risk and the misaligned 72h counter (https://craevidence.com/cra-compliance/enisa-srp-onboarding). An ENISA survey found 20% of SMEs were unsure the CRA even applied to them (https://www.techtarget.com/cybersecurity/feature/EU-Cyber-Resilience-Act-reporting-What-CISOs-need-to-know). Greenbone's readiness review found the platform still in testing two weeks before go-live and no standards published (https://www.greenbone.net/en/blog/cra-article-14-readiness-status/). ENISA launch note: https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/the-cra-single-reporting-platform-is-launched.
first_30_days: Turn the public ENISA and Commission material into a free 'SRP pre-flight' checklist and a 24h/72h clock template, and publish both. Recruit 4-6 freelance product-security engineers across EU, US and Asia time zones for a rotation. Cold-message about 300 product-security, CE-compliance and CTO contacts at hardware makers (RED and CE registries, hardware crowdfunding lists). Offer 5 founding pilots at EUR 99 per month plus a free first drill. Book a tabletop drill with each pilot and convert the drill output into the case study.

title: Surety Bonds for Agent Operators
one_liner: A customs bond for bots: agent operators post a surety-backed bond so sites, APIs and merchants can say yes to their agents and get paid if the agents misbehave.
customer: Mid-size vendors of browser, shopping and procurement agents ($1M-$50M ARR) whose agents get blocked or throttled. They pay for the bond and credential. Merchants and API providers consume the signal for free.
problem: Agent identity schemes (signed agents, know-your-agent) say who an agent is, not who pays when it scrapes abusively, mis-buys or triggers chargebacks. Agents are cheap to recreate, so identity carries no cost of failure. Bots are now 57.4% of requests, so sites default to blocking. After the August 2026 Ninth Circuit Comet ruling, blocking has to rest on contract and technical measures, so sites need a concrete reason to let agents in.
solution: Underwrite the operator (KYB, behavior review, volume caps). Issue a surety or insurer-backed bond ($25k-$1M penal sum) plus a signed credential that plugs into existing agent-auth headers and protocols. Sites whitelist a bonded lane with higher rate limits. A small claims desk pays on signed request logs. Wedge: agent vendors selling into mid-market merchants and B2B API providers that would create a bonded lane in their bot rules.
why_now: Bots overtook humans in 2026, and the Ninth Circuit ruling shifts blocking to contract terms. Neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding agent-dispute rule, and Visa's merchant dispute threshold tightened to 1.5% in April 2026, so merchants are risk-averse. Bonding has been proposed only in academic papers so far, and no product exists.
revenue_model: Bond premium share (typically 1-3% of penal sum per year) plus a $500-$5,000/month underwriting and credential fee, plus surety agency commission.
non_obvious_insight: Trust that scales in commerce rests on bonds, not identity. Freight brokers, contractors and customs brokers all post bonds. A bond makes an operator's reputation costly to abandon, and a site only has to trust the surety, not the operator.
first_30_days: Partner with a small surety agency or MGA to draft a miscellaneous bond form and a claims evidence standard. Recruit 5 agent vendors that merchants block and 5 merchants or API providers willing to whitelist. Sell the first 3 pilot bonds at $500-$1,500 per year plus a setup fee.

title: Master-Leased Housing to Recruit Care Workers Domestically
one_liner: Asset-light staff housing near care facilities that lets operators recruit domestic workers from a wider radius, starting with stranded worker apartments.
customer: Nursing homes, assisted-living and memory-care operators (5-40 sites) and home-care agencies in tight labor markets such as Wisconsin and rural areas.
problem: The visa pause cuts off the overseas pipeline. Direct care workers are paid little (66% earn under $35k), so domestic recruits can't afford to relocate to where beds are staffed. Closed beds and wings in Wisconsin show the cost. Turnover of 77-80% means every hire has to be retained.
solution: Master-lease or take over apartments near facilities, furnish them, and sublease bed by bed to employees at below-market rent. Employers fund the gap ($300-600 per bed per month) under a guarantee. Add a 3-month 'landing pad' with transport, CNA certification and ESL classes, and a relocation pipeline from oversupplied labor markets (laid-off retail and hospitality workers).
why_now: Wisconsin nursing homes spent $100k+ on apartments for overseas workers and then abandoned the plan when visa access closed, so there are stranded assets to take over. About 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4, and about one in five immigrant direct-care workers come from countries hit by the 75-country visa pause.
revenue_model: Per-bed monthly management margin ($100-200 on top of rent), employer subsidy, and a $1,500 placement fee per hire retained at 90 days.
non_obvious_insight: When foreign labor is cut off, housing rather than wages becomes the binding constraint to domestic recruitment. A 20-bed closed wing loses over $1M a year in revenue, so a $7k a year housing subsidy per worker is trivially worth it.
first_30_days: Approach the Wisconsin operators who bought apartments and offer to operate and re-let them to domestic hires. Run a 12-bed pilot in one town with two operators and track time-to-fill and 90-day retention.

title: Medicaid Work-Rule Retention for Hospitals and Plans
one_liner: A text-first service that proves work hours and exemptions on behalf of Medicaid members, paid per retained member by the hospitals and health plans that would otherwise lose them.
customer: Safety-net hospitals, FQHC networks and Medicaid managed-care plans in expansion states. They pay roughly $4-12 per retained member per month or a fee per successful report.
problem: Under the 2025 budget law (OBBBA), expansion adults aged 19-64 must document about 80 hours a month of work, school or volunteering, or prove an exemption, with more frequent renewals. Deadlines start no later than January 1, 2027, with limited state extensions. Arkansas in 2018 showed that people mostly lost coverage from reporting failures, not from ineligibility. Members lose coverage over paperwork. Hospitals and plans then lose revenue and absorb uncompensated care.
solution: A retention layer that sits on the member side. It works over SMS and WhatsApp in multiple languages. It connects to the member's payroll, gig-platform earnings, school enrollment or caregiver records to auto-assemble monthly proof. It screens for the many exemptions (medically frail, parents of young children, substance-use treatment, recent release) and generates provider attestation letters from the clinic's own visit. It submits in each state's format, using portal automation and mail-in where needed. It nags before deadlines. A dashboard shows the plan or hospital which members are at risk before the coverage cliff. The same engine later covers SNAP work rules.
why_now: The law was signed in July 2025, and federal guidance and state build-outs are happening now for the 2027 start. Some states, such as Georgia with Pathways, already run work-reporting programs. The large incumbents (state-agency contractors) build for the state side, not for retention on the member side. Hospital CFOs are modeling large expansion-population losses this budget cycle. LLM agents plus computer-use can drive dozens of clunky state portals that never had APIs. Gig and payroll data connections make proof of hours automatic.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month retention fee, or per-successful-report fee, paid by hospitals, FQHCs and plans. Later, state contracts and a SNAP work-requirement product on the same infrastructure.
non_obvious_insight: The payer is neither the patient nor the state. It is whoever loses revenue when a member drops. The failure is documentation friction, not eligibility. The cheapest evidence source is the member's own gig or payroll account plus the clinic visit itself, which can collect exemption proof for free.
first_30_days: Choose one state with an early or waiver-driven start and a large FQHC association. Meet revenue-cycle and financial-counseling leads at 5 FQHCs and hospitals. Publish a free state-by-state 'Am I exempt? Do my hours count?' checker to generate leads. Run a manual SMS concierge pilot with 200 members using a spreadsheet and volunteers, and measure on-time reporting rate. Convert the best result into a signed letter of intent for a per-retained-member fee.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Public Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee audit that finds 'tariff surcharge' line items on city, school-district, transit and university purchase orders and recovers the share vendors are now being refunded after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs.
customer: County and city finance departments, school districts, transit agencies, public universities and public hospitals. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered and nothing upfront.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026. Roughly 330,000 importers paid about $166B, and as of July only about $86B had been repaid, so about $80B remained outstanding. Refunds go to the importer of record, not to the public buyers who paid vendor surcharges (one machine-shop supplier surcharge was 2.7%). Small importers and delivered-duty-unpaid shipments, including many university and hospital equipment imports, are likely to go unclaimed. Brokers are paid per entry and have no reason to chase this.
solution: Step 1: mine open-checkbook portals to rank vendors in tariff-exposed categories (school buses, HVAC, lab equipment, IT, furniture, playgrounds) and file public-records requests for their invoices to find surcharge lines. Step 2: send standardized pass-through refund claims and negotiate credit memos where the contract or surcharge language supports it. Step 3: where the public entity was itself importer of record (DDU), file its own refund claims. A dashboard tracks vendor refund status and the client's recovered dollars.
why_now: Refunds are flowing in phases now, with liquidated-entry and AD/CVD cases coming later, so vendor cash is fresh but memory of surcharges will fade. Claim deadlines and statutes of limitation close within 12-18 months. Public entities are under budget pressure and readily accept no-cost recovery audits, as with utility-bill and sales-tax audits.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a lower fee on refunds recovered by filing as importer of record. The same platform later runs recurring price-escalation monitoring for a subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The money sits with a party who has no incentive to hand it over, while the party who bore the cost has unusual leverage: public buyers can demand transparency, make supplier performance part of the record, and threaten future award eligibility. Public procurement contracts and open-checkbook data make targets findable without any client cooperation.
first_30_days: Pull open-checkbook data for 3 states, file about 30 public-records requests for surcharge invoices, and have counsel review a standard claim letter. Cold-email 20 finance directors with a personalized 'you likely overpaid $X to Vendor Y' one-pager and sign two pilots on contingency.

title: Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases
one_liner: White-label filing infrastructure that lets solo immigration lawyers file mandamus/APA delay lawsuits in 48 hours, turning the government's habit of mooting suits into a flat-fee product.
customer: Solo and small immigration firms (1-10 attorneys) who pay a per-filing platform fee; end clients (naturalization, green card and employment petition applicants) pay the firm a flat $2.5-5k. Secondary buyer: employers with stuck petitions.
problem: Cases are stuck well past posted processing times: interviewed N-400s never scheduled for oath, I-485s and I-140s idling, and holds or pauses applied to nationals of dozens of countries since late 2025. Clients wait 12-30 months. Lawyers know a federal delay suit often shakes a case loose, but most solos have never filed one. Drafting the complaint, civil cover sheet, summons, service on the U.S. Attorney's civil process clerk, the Attorney General and the agency, and district-specific local rules is a 6-10 hour learning curve, and no one wants to be the first to file.
solution: A web tool with three parts. (1) An eligibility screen: enter the receipt date, form type and field office, and it compares them to posted times and to real observed outcomes, then scores the delay claim. (2) A complaint and exhibit generator with a per-district rules library, a service-of-process checklist and deadline calendar (the 60-day government answer window), and a template for the joint status report or stipulated dismissal that follows adjudication. (3) A docket-outcome database that logs, by district, judge and case type, how long from filing to adjudication. The attorney of record signs every filing. The platform is software, not a law firm.
why_now: Through late 2025 and 2026 USCIS added enhanced vetting, holds and pauses on benefit requests tied to nationality, expanded re-review of approved cases, and slower naturalization and green card scheduling. The volume of genuinely stuck cases is at a decade high. Federal courts are also less deferential to agencies since the Loper Bright decision, and adjudicating a stuck case is cheaper for the government than defending it. Solos are overloaded and short of billable-hour alternatives, so a ready-made product for a high-ticket service is easy to sell.
revenue_model: $350-600 per filing charged to the law firm (flat, not a percentage, to avoid fee-splitting rules), or $299/month for up to 3 filings. Later: a paid intelligence tier of docket-outcome analytics by district, and a litigation-funding partnership for clients who can't front the fee.
non_obvious_insight: The lawsuit is rarely litigated to judgment. The U.S. Attorney's Office usually tells USCIS to adjudicate within 30-90 days so the suit can be dismissed as moot, so the client's real purchase is a forced deadline. Clients almost never hear about this because form-prep firms earn on the application, not on pressure. Posted processing times are also misleading (they reflect only completed cases at a percentile), so whoever accumulates real time-to-decision data by field office and district owns the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 immigration attorneys in high-volume districts (N.D. Cal., S.D. Tex., D.N.J., E.D.N.Y., S.D. Fla.) and offer free templates for the first filing. Build the intake screen and three complaint templates first (delayed N-400 after interview, delayed I-485, delayed I-130/I-140 or a nationality hold). Concierge-run 10 filings by hand, charging the firms $400 each. Log every outcome date, since that dataset is the product. Post outcome stats to immigration-lawyer Facebook groups and AILA chapter listservs to pull in the next 30 firms.

title: Immune-Training Forest-Floor Yards for Daycares
one_liner: A certified installation and refill service that replaces sterile daycare yards with vetted forest floor and sod to diversify children's skin and gut microbiota.
customer: Private daycare chains, preschool operators, nature-based preschools and municipal early-childhood departments in cities, especially ones competing on parent trust and outdoor programming.
problem: Allergies, asthma and immune disorders are rising in urban kids, who spend 8+ hours a day in daycare yards of plastic, gravel and rubber mulch with almost no microbial diversity. Parents worry, but the options are vague 'nature play' features with no evidence of health impact.
solution: Biodiversity kits based on the Finnish protocol: about 100 m2 of pathogen-screened forest floor litter and 200 m2 of sod, planter boxes and simple play rules, sourced from vetted local woodland. We add a seasonal refill and an optional microbiome swab study, all under a 'Biodiversity Certified' badge that daycares can show to parents.
why_now: There is direct peer-reviewed evidence. In a study of 10 Finnish daycares with 75 children aged 3-5, adding forest floor and sod for 28 days changed skin and gut microbiota and immune markers (Roslund et al., Science Advances, 2020), and a 2021 follow-up on long-term effects was published. Parents are more microbiome-aware, and cities are funding cooling and greening of schoolyards.
revenue_model: One-time install of roughly $6-15k per yard plus an annual refill subscription of roughly $1-2k per year, since the biology decays and litter needs replacing. Licensing of the certification badge to chains, and public-tender revenue from cities.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody can patent dirt, so the moat is safe sourcing, pathogen testing and certification, and the recurring consumable makes it a regional supply chain of local ecological material. Selling 'immune infrastructure' to childcare works because the buyer's real problem is parent trust, and a visible, evidence-backed feature beats a marketing claim.
first_30_days: Contact 10 forest schools and one small chain. Build a 30 m2 pilot with a local soil scientist and a university microbiologist for about $1.5k. Set up a baseline and follow-up swab pilot and sell the first three paid yards to chains that want a differentiator.

title: Ticketmaster Exit Kits for Independent Venues
one_liner: A contract-audit and migration service that tells venue owners exactly when and at what cost they can leave exclusive ticketing deals, then moves them safely.
customer: Independent venue owners and operators of 500-3,000 capacity rooms in the US, and promoters who run pre-sales through those venues.
problem: A jury found Live Nation liable for illegal monopolization on 2026-04-15, and remedies remain unclear (a separate DOJ settlement dates from 2026-03-09). Venues with exclusive contracts do not know what leaving costs (liquidated damages, advance repayment, loss of fan data), and fear a botched on-sale day more than the contract.
solution: A contract analyzer that reads exclusivity, term, advance-repayment and change-of-law clauses and returns an exit date and cost sheet. Add a migration playbook (fan data export with consent, fee structure compliant with the FTC all-in rule, verified-fan pre-sales), white-label integrations with 2-3 alternative ticketing platforms, and pooled negotiation for groups of venues.
why_now: The April 2026 verdict, the FTC's all-in pricing rule (effective 2025-05-12), the state suits, and Ticketmaster's June 2026 placement inside Spotify all raise the stakes of lock-in. Venues suddenly have leverage but no capability.
revenue_model: $2-5k audit, $5-15k migration, and 10-20% of alternative platforms' fee share on the venue's tickets for three years.
non_obvious_insight: Antitrust wins create optionality, not capability. The bottleneck after a verdict is the GM's fear of a broken on-sale, so the product to sell is reduced fear, plus data ownership the venue never knew it lacked.
first_30_days: Mine the public trial exhibits for venue-contract terms and publish an exit map. Reach 10 venue GMs through independent-venue trade groups. Run three paid contract audits at $1.5k and line up two alternative ticketing partners.

title: Repatriation-of-Remains Concierge for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A fixed-price service that gets a loved one's body home across borders, and later a low-cost membership that pre-funds it.
customer: Immigrant families on one corridor at a time (for example US to Mexico or Central America, the Philippines, India or Nigeria), plus consulates, churches, mosques, community associations and funeral homes without international skills.
problem: Sending remains home costs thousands (often $5-15K, unverified) and requires consular paperwork, health permits, embalming, sealed caskets, air cargo rules and destination-side logistics. Families use GoFundMe, church collections and opaque middlemen, in days, while grieving.
solution: Intake in the family's language, document assembly (consulate forms, permits), a vetted network of embalmers, cargo forwarders and destination funeral homes, insurance and payment plans, and one coordinator. Later add a $8-$15/month repatriation membership underwritten through a licensed insurer partner.
why_now: Community payment and remittance rails are digital, translation and document assembly are cheap with AI, and immigrant communities are large and trust-network driven. Funeral homes treat this as an add-on they don't understand.
revenue_model: 15-25% service margin on $6-12K cases, membership fees, and insurer commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The mainstream industry treats repatriation as a sideline, but for these families it is the primary product. Corridor-specific know-how is the moat, and trust travels through churches and consulates.
first_30_days: Choose one corridor and one metro. Partner with a funeral home that already does it. Sign 3 churches or a consulate liaison. Run 5 cases at cost to document the exact process and price it.

title: Human-Backed Login for Senior-Serving Software
one_liner: A drop-in login layer for apps whose users are 65+ that replaces passwords with a two-tap flow, a spoken one-time code by phone call (landline included), family delegates and a live concierge who can walk anyone in.
customer: Vertical SaaS vendors whose users are older adults: senior-living and home-care family portals, community and church software, benefits and Medicare-broker portals, pharmacy and telehealth apps, funeral-planning tools. They pay about $0.80-2 per active senior per month, $3 per concierge-assisted login, with a $299/month minimum.
problem: An operator of a ~10-year-old SaaS used heavily by people 65+ says users 'are tired and frustrated about remembering the domain/path to login screen and then which email/password they used', and that simplification has not fixed it. The 60 responses show what fails: forced resets, masked passwords, magic links (older users struggle switching apps), QR codes and passkeys. What people say they'd pay for is a human: 'elderly individuals want a solution rather than a lesson', and a 'code that you can type in on another device... my grandmother could call and read me a code'.
solution: Per-customer short vanity login URL plus a large 'Call me' button that triggers a phone call reading a short code aloud, working for landlines and flip phones, then persistent trusted-device sessions that effectively never log out. A family-delegate approve/reset flow, no forced password rotation, and no masked fields by default. When automation fails, a live concierge line verifies identity via vendor-supplied challenge questions and completes recovery. Ship as an SDK/widget plus hosted pages, with audit logs suitable for HIPAA-adjacent customers, and report the reduction in login-related support tickets per customer.
why_now: Big platforms pushed passkeys to consumers in 2025-2026 and older users, and the relatives who support them, are loudly reporting confusion and lockouts. The same vendors are under pressure to support MFA. Telephony APIs make voice-delivered codes cheap, and support cost per senior user is the metric operators feel.
revenue_model: Per-active-senior monthly fee, per-assisted-login fee for concierge calls, $299/month minimum, and an annual contract with an ticket-reduction guarantee for larger vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Authentication products optimize against attackers; for the 65+ user the dominant failure is support cost and churn, and the operators in the thread say the answer they would pay for is a human plus a code they can read out loud, not a better protocol. Every fashionable option (passkeys, magic links, QR) was named as failing for this group in the same thread. Evidence: Ask HN 'Easiest UX for Seniors', 58 points, 60 comments https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47729327; passkey confusion for elderly relatives and recovery gaps https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49010448.
first_30_days: Wire Twilio Verify's voice channel to a hosted 'Call me to log in' page and staff a three-person phone shift. Pitch 20 founders of senior-vertical SaaS (found via LinkedIn and association vendor directories), starting with the Ask HN author. Offer a $299/month 60-day pilot that measures login-related support tickets before and after, and convert on a shown reduction.

title: Half-Plate Menus for GLP-1 Diners
one_liner: A menu-engineering and POS program that turns GLP-1 diners into incremental visits through protein-first half portions.
customer: Multi-unit casual-dining and fast-casual operators with 20-300 locations.
problem: GLP-1 households cut restaurant spend about 8%, yet 48% of users say they would dine out more if smaller portions were offered.
solution: Design a 'Half-Plate' section (65-70% of full price, protein-forward, fiber-tuned), integrate it in the POS, and measure incremental visits and margin per cover.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use a GLP-1 and the oral Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 at $149-299/month, so the segment is now big enough for a dedicated menu line.
revenue_model: Per-location monthly fee plus a performance share of measured incremental visits.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume smaller portions cannibalize revenue, but restaurant labor and rent are per-cover costs. A visit at 70% of the check with lower food cost beats losing the visit at 100%.
first_30_days: Sign two regional chains for a 10-store test of a Half-Plate section and set up a simple visit-frequency and basket dashboard from POS exports.

title: Bone-First Strength Program for Women 45+
one_liner: A gym-delivered lifting and impact program for perimenopausal women, sold on DEXA-verified bone and muscle results.
customer: Women aged roughly 42-60 paying $79-149 per month, delivered through independent gyms, Pilates and strength studios and PT clinics that license the program.
problem: Women's fitness tech is fixated on cycle-syncing even though current evidence for cycle effects on performance is inconclusive, while midlife women (an 'invisible cohort' in sports science) face accelerating bone and muscle loss, worsened for those on GLP-1 drugs. Gyms sell toning and never measure the outcome that matters.
solution: A 24-week program of progressive heavy lifting, impact and balance work, with DEXA at baseline, 6 and 12 months via partner scan providers, simple bone-loading dose tracking with a hip or wrist sensor, coach training and a results dashboard studios use for retention. Positioned as wellness and performance with a physician advisor, not treatment.
why_now: Retail DEXA scans have dropped to roughly sub-$100, menopause is a mainstream topic, wearable makers are pouring money into women's health, perimenopause research is accelerating in 2026, and GLP-1 adoption has made bone and lean-mass loss a mass-market worry.
revenue_model: Member fees $79-149 per month; studio license $299-499 per month plus $30 per member; scan affiliate margin of $10-20 per scan.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is the outcome measurement: 'X percent of members held or gained bone density at 12 months' is a claim no gym can currently make, and the resulting dataset is valuable to clinicians and researchers. Cycle-syncing is a distraction from the larger midlife need.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 women aged 45-60 through two local strength gyms, book baseline DEXA scans with a retail or mobile provider, run a 12-week pilot with a physician advisor, and sign three studios to license the program off the interim results.

title: Shared Certified Operators for Tiny Water Systems
one_liner: A marketplace pairing retired and semi-retired certified water operators with mobile-home parks, small towns and rural systems that must legally have one and cannot hire one.
customer: Mobile-home parks, towns under 3,300 people, rural water districts, and schools, campgrounds and churches on their own wells. They pay $600 to $2,500 a month per system. Supply side: retired plant operators, and operators laid off by consolidations.
problem: Regulations require a state-certified operator in responsible charge. Roughly 30% to 50% of the workforce is retiring within a decade, small systems cannot offer a full-time salary, and losing the operator means violations, fines and boil notices. New lead and PFAS monitoring adds workload.
solution: Vet and license-match operators state by state, pair each with a cluster of 8 to 12 nearby systems, and run telemetry-based oversight (cheap chlorine-residual, tank-level and pump-current sensors) so the certified person supervises remotely while a local non-certified lead hand does routine tasks. The platform handles state contract-operator paperwork, liability insurance, scheduling and compliance reporting.
why_now: Retirements are hitting small systems hardest. Cheap LTE-M and satellite-capable water sensors make remote supervision affordable. Public SDWIS violation data provides a ready-made, ranked lead list.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer per system with the platform keeping 25% to 35%. Sensor kit resale or lease at about $1,500. Insurance and compliance-reporting add-ons. Later: state programs paying to reduce violations.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not labor hours; it is the legal signature of a certified operator. One operator with telemetry can responsibly oversee ten tiny systems, and the regulator's own violations database is the sales list.
first_30_days: Pull SDWIS operator-certification and monitoring violations for one state. Recruit 3 retired operators via the state operator association. Sign 3 to 5 mobile-home parks at about $750 a month with compliant contract-operator letters and install a $1.5k telemetry kit.

title: The 4 A.M. Ride Guild
one_liner: A dispatch network of night-owl local drivers, paid per ride by hospitals and jails, that gets rural patients and released inmates home at hours when Uber and Medicaid rides do not exist.
customer: Critical access hospitals and their foundations, county jails, domestic violence shelters, crisis stabilization units, and Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans (through value-added benefits). Paid per ride, then by plan contract.
problem: A patient is discharged from a rural ER at 4am. She came by ambulance, her car is 30 miles away, and no taxi, Uber or Lyft exists. Medicaid non-emergency transport needs 24-48 hours notice and does not cover ER discharge. So she sits in the waiting room, a nurse drives her home (against policy), a relative is woken up, or the hospital admits her to observation for 'social reasons', which costs thousands. Jails release people at midnight with no ride, and domestic violence shelters have the same problem in reverse.
solution: A dispatch line (an SMS and phone flow with a human on call, then an app) that promises a driver within 30 minutes anywhere in a county between 10pm and 8am. Supply comes from people who are awake anyway: workers finishing third shift at plants, retired EMTs, volunteer firefighters and off-duty deputies. Riders can be dropped at a hospital, home or shelter, with documented handoff for CMS discharge planning. Add wheelchair-capable vehicles later. Insurance is hired and non-owned auto coverage, and drivers are background checked.
why_now: Rural hospitals are under pressure from Medicaid cuts and closing service lines, so avoiding costly observation stays and unsafe discharges matters more. Rural Health Transformation Program funds can pay for transport and access. Uber Health, Lyft and NEMT brokers are still thin at rural night hours, and the gap is a supply problem software alone cannot fix. Gig-style dispatch and background-check tooling is now cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: The hospital pays $85-110 per ride and the driver gets $55-65. A monthly minimum of $500-1,500 per facility guarantees driver availability, similar to a retainer. Later add Medicaid MCO and Medicare Advantage value-added benefit contracts. The ride log also supports the hospital's safe-discharge documentation.
non_obvious_insight: Nurses know that the ride is what actually gates a safe discharge at night, and that the hospital quietly pays for it in nurse gas money, observation admissions and ambulance runs. Transport startups assume demand is the hard part. In rural night hours supply is the hard part, and the winning move is recruiting people who are awake at 4am and paying them a guaranteed minimum. Hospital foundations, whose donors like 'getting Grandma home safe', are also a surprisingly easy first funder.
first_30_days: Sign one hospital and one sheriff's office for a pilot with a prepaid $1,000 retainer each. Recruit 15 drivers through third-shift plants, fire department Facebook groups and truck stops. Run dispatch manually via a Twilio group text with the founder on call. Get a hired-and-non-owned auto policy through a commercial broker and run background checks through a screening vendor. Track time to ride and observation stays avoided, and use those to pitch a second and third hospital.

title: Insurability Passport Attached to California Home Listings
one_liner: A pre-listing report that verifies wildfire mitigation and attaches bindable insurance options (FAIR Plan plus wraparound, admitted where available) to the listing, so buyers see the real insured cost before they make an offer.
customer: Listing agents and sellers in California wildfire-exposed ZIP codes, paying $149-299 per listing. MGAs and agencies pay commissions on policies that bind from the passport.
problem: Buyers, lenders and agents cannot tell before contract whether a house can be insured or at what price. The FAIR Plan grew to 696,562 policies and $768B of exposure by June 2026 (up 157% since September 2022). Seven of California's twelve largest insurers have stopped writing new business or renewing. Deals slip or die when insurance is discovered in escrow.
solution: A listing add-on that combines a mitigation inspection (Zone 0, vents, roof, photos), an insurability status by carrier type, and indicative premiums for FAIR Plan plus a difference-in-conditions wrap, and admitted quotes where they exist. It also identifies the cheapest mitigation actions that would change eligibility or price. The seller shows a QR code on the listing, and buyers can bind from the passport.
why_now: The California Department of Insurance is pushing the FAIR Plan to offer broader comprehensive coverage (Make It FAIR Act, AB 1680, announced 2026-02-02). Liberty Mutual and Safeco began nonrenewing California condo and renter policies from 2026-01-01. The state also mandates wildfire safety discounts for verified mitigation.
revenue_model: Listing fee of $149-299 for the passport. Commission on bound policies through a partner agency or MGA (typically 10-15% of premium). Optional referral fees from mitigation contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance availability is being handled after the offer, in escrow, although it decides affordability at the moment of offer. Evidence: the FAIR Plan's own key statistics page shows 696,562 policies, $768B exposure and 'fewer coverage options available' in the voluntary market (https://www.cfpnet.com/key-statistics-data/). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_FAIR_Plan lists seven of twelve top insurers pausing new business or renewals. https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/west/2024/12/20/328011.htm shows Safeco and Liberty Mutual leaving condo and renters lines, with nonrenewals beginning 2026-01-01. https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release005-2026.cfm describes the pending FAIR Plan coverage overhaul. Pre-listing home inspections became a normal seller expense; an insurability passport is the next one, and the mitigation data feeds the moratorium idea above. The main risk is that carrier and FAIR Plan quoting cannot be automated quickly, so start with manual agent-assisted quotes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 listing agents in Altadena, Sierra Madre, Santa Rosa and Bay Area WUI markets. Partner with one independent agency that quotes FAIR Plan plus DIC. Build a one-page passport (photos, mitigation checklist, three quote scenarios) and deliver it manually for 10 listings at a launch price of $99. Track how many escrows it saves and use those cases to raise the price.

title: Loss-Draft as a Service for Servicers
one_liner: After a hail or wildfire claim, insurer money is trapped in slow servicer loss-draft processes. Digitize milestone releases so contractors get paid in days, not months.
customer: Mortgage servicers' loss-draft departments, and roofing and repair contractors who work insurance claims.
problem: Insurance claim checks are co-payable to the mortgage lender. Servicers hold the funds and release them in draws after inspections, taking weeks to months. Contractors demand money upfront, homeowners run out of patience, and disputes spread (State Farm hail-claim lawsuits are widening from Oklahoma).
solution: Digital loss-draft. The homeowner uploads the claim payment, funds sit in a servicer-controlled escrow, and milestone releases are verified via geo-tagged photo and video review. Contractors are paid instantly via RTP or FedNow, and the servicer gets a compliance dashboard on cycle times.
why_now: Claim disputes are surging and State Farm is adding 3,000 claims staff (Insurance Journal, 2026-09-25). Instant rails are mature, and servicers face regulatory scrutiny on loss-mitigation timelines (verify the specific rules).
revenue_model: $150-$400 per claim from the servicer, or 0.5-1.0% of proceeds, plus a 1% instant-pay fee to contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Servicers hold large claim balances but run loss-draft as a paper-heavy cost center. Contractors accept lower prices for fast, certain payment, which also lowers repair cost and dispute rates.
first_30_days: Approach five mid-size servicers' loss-draft heads with a free diagnostic on average days to disbursement. Sign a pilot for one catastrophe event. Recruit roofing contractor associations in hail-prone states to onboard.

title: Vendor-neutral body-cam redaction bureau with fee pass-through
one_liner: A CJIS-cleared remote team that returns double-reviewed redacted police video priced per minute below the fee small cities already charge requesters, so the bureau funds itself.
customer: Small police departments and sheriff's offices (roughly 5-60 sworn officers) with records backlogs, and the city clerks and attorneys who carry the liability. They pay $0.40-0.60 per video minute plus a small monthly minimum.
problem: Small agencies do not have redaction staff. Elko, NV's police chief described about a year of catching up on redaction requests with no full-time redaction team and approved a five-year Axon extension of about $91,200 a year. White Salmon, WA has only two trained employees and set a $0.84-per-minute redaction fee (4-1 vote, April 15, 2026) while the chief said he 'cannot readily add a second-review step for all releases' because of limited trained staff and high request volume. A councilor dissented, arguing that sensitive footage such as juveniles needs more than one reviewer. Phoenix has nearly 40,000 pending public-records requests and raised commercial fees to pay for staff. AI-generated request floods (Somerset County, PA saw dozens a day) make it worse.
solution: A regional redaction bureau. Departments send only the clips requested (through share links from Axon, Motorola/WatchGuard, Getac and Wolfcom or others) and get back redacted video plus a redaction log within 5 business days. Automated face, plate and audio detection does the first pass. Then two trained human reviewers sign off, with a state-specific checklist (juveniles, victims, medical, informants). The bureau also sells 'backlog amnesty sprints' at a flat rate to clear a year-old queue. Vendor neutrality is the selling point, since Axon's automated redaction only helps agencies inside its ecosystem and still requires manual verification.
why_now: Body camera adoption is nearly universal after 2025-2026 contract cycles (Elko, Plainview, Crescent City, Carlsbad, Kasson approvals), public-records volume is up, and states are formalizing per-minute cost recovery. Councils are now adopting the fee schedules that make a pass-through model possible.
revenue_model: Per-minute fee ($0.40-0.60) billed to the agency, which recovers most or all of it from requesters at its own per-minute fee (White Salmon: $0.84); monthly minimum of $250; flat-rate backlog sprints of $5k-20k.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not blurring speed, it is a defensible second review on sensitive content, which small departments cannot staff. The fee schedule councils are adopting is derived from a cost-of-service study, so the department can pass the bureau's cost straight through; the bureau's margin lies between its price and the city's published fee. CJIS clearance and background checks form the moat that keeps generic video-AI startups out. Evidence: Elko's year-long backlog (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog); White Salmon's two trained employees, the $0.84/minute fee and the second-review dissent (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8492326/washington/klickitat-county/white-salmon/council-updates-public-records-policy-approves-084-per-minute-body-camera-redaction-fee-over-staff-objections); Phoenix's roughly 40,000 pending requests (https://www.kjzz.org/politics/2026-09-24/commercial-public-records-requests-prices-have-gone-up-in-phoenix-in-effort-to-hire-more-staff).
first_30_days: Pick one state, such as Washington, with strong public-records laws and many small departments. Sign the CJIS security addendum with 2 agencies and have all reviewers fingerprint-cleared. Find 15 departments with a visible backlog in recent council minutes and offer a flat 'backlog amnesty sprint' on their first 500 minutes at $0.45/min. Turn the state's checklist into a review template and deliver the first 3 jobs within the month.

title: Buyer-Side RFP Claim Verifier for Cities
one_liner: Automated reference-checking and claim-testing for the flood of AI-polished bids that city procurement offices cannot separate.
customer: Procurement offices at cities, counties, school districts and cooperative purchasing bodies with lean staff, plus state procurement agencies.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write RFPs and vendors use AI to answer them, so every response looks perfect. Dallas County is cutting IT staff. Only 5.3% of AI-related contract provisions address transparency, and local tech contracts average 7 years. A bad pick locks the city in.
solution: Ingest bids, extract every checkable claim (reference customers, uptime, certifications, incident history, prior contracts) and verify against public records, contract databases, court dockets, security advisories and automated outreach to references. Deliver a one-page evidence-scored comparison that the evaluation committee can attach to the award file.
why_now: The vendor-side tools (NationGraph raised $22.5M to help vendors read documents and write proposals) have collapsed the signal in bids. Michigan's fraud-system disaster ($20M settlement plus $78M replacement) has made buyers nervous.
revenue_model: $1.5-5K per RFP for small buyers, or annual subscription for a state or co-op ($25-100K). A per-audit fee for high-risk software and AI awards.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is selling to the vendor who is writing. The scarce, budgeted, blame-averse buyer is the one drowning in identical documents and has no tool that raises the cost of lying.
first_30_days: Take five closed public RFPs and publish a teardown showing which claims failed verification. Offer free pre-award checks to 5 county procurement offices. Charge from the second use.

title: Farm-to-Factory Water Supply Assurance
one_liner: A diligence-plus-settlement service that sells expanding plants a permit-grade, verified acre-foot supply by leasing fallowed farm water in drought-stressed Western basins.
customer: Plant developers, site-selection teams and economic-development agencies for semiconductor, pharma and food plants in AZ, TX, ID and UT. Irrigation districts and farmers are the supply side.
problem: Water is now a siting gate: Texas froze grid connections over water, the Colorado River's 2027-2036 framework forces farm cuts, and Amazon put $20M into farm conservation with no settlement layer. Factories need a legally defensible supply and 'water neutral' commitments, and farmers cannot easily sell verified savings.
solution: Start with a $15-40k water-supply diligence report (rights, drought exposure, discharge capacity, PFAS in source). Then structure and meter option-style leases with farmers, with satellite and meter verification, and issue an assurance letter usable in permitting.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Colorado River Record of Decision, 49.6% of the US in drought, and reshoring in water-intensive sectors (electronics +35%, pharma +32%, food +17% in robot orders) collide.
revenue_model: Diligence fee plus 5-8% of lease flow and a verification fee per acre-foot.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest new industrial water supply is a farmer's fallowed field, but only if someone provides the paperwork that turns it into a permit-grade asset.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Pinal, AZ). Sign three farmers on non-binding option terms. Sell two diligence reports to plant real-estate teams or EDCs, and recruit a water-rights attorney as an advisor.

title: Live Lyric Captions for Concerts
one_liner: Setlist-conditioned real-time captions of sung lyrics and banter, delivered to phones and smart glasses with translation, sold to venues as an accessibility service.
customer: Venues, festivals and touring promoters with accessibility obligations, plus artists wanting international fans served.
problem: Deaf and hard-of-hearing fans get no lyrics, because speech recognition fails on singing over a loud PA. Human captioning exists for spoken theatre but not concerts, and overseas fans lack translation.
solution: Load the artist's setlist and lyrics ahead of time. Align the sound-desk audio to lyrics with tolerance for improvisation and run speech recognition only on banter. Distribute via a QR-code web page and smart glasses with per-language translation, with a human captioner supervising deviations.
why_now: Display-equipped smart glasses started shipping in late 2025, on-device translation is good enough, and venues face growing accessibility pressure.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per show for venues plus a paid translation tier from artists' fan clubs, and sponsorship from device makers.
non_obvious_insight: Lyrics are the one thing known in advance, which turns an impossible speech recognition problem into a tractable alignment problem. Accessibility budgets exist but nobody sells a concert-native product.
first_30_days: Test at 3 local shows with two Deaf community groups. Partner with one venue for a free pilot, gather testimonials, and sign 2 venues at $250 per month.

title: Post-Montgomery Walk-Around Audits for Freight Brokers
one_liner: A gig network of working and retired truckers who physically inspect the carriers a broker hires and hand back a lawyer-ready diligence file.
customer: Mid-size freight brokers and 3PLs ($50M to $1B gross bookings, 10 to 200 staff). The budget owner is the VP of compliance/risk or general counsel. Secondary buyers are contingent-auto and broker E&O underwriters, and shippers that run in-house brokerage.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-selection suits against brokers are not preempted by federal law. Brokers now have to prove they exercised reasonable care picking a carrier. Their vetting is entirely digital: SAFER lookups, insurance certificates, ID checks. Nobody has ever looked at the yard. Chameleon carriers with clean paperwork, fake addresses and fictitious pickups sail through, and so do genuinely dangerous small fleets. Verisk CargoNet put Q2 2026 theft losses at $304.6M, more than double Q2 2025, even though incident counts fell.
solution: Book a 45-minute physical walk-around of a carrier's listed terminal, yard or the driver's truck for $175 to $350. The trucker follows a 40-point protocol and shoots geo-stamped photo and video: steer tire tread and sidewall damage, brake chamber stroke, lights, ELD present and working, trailer age and VIN against registration, whether the address has a shop, lot and signage, and a two-minute driver interview. The broker gets a scored, reproducible report filed against the carrier ID. Upsells are a quarterly re-walk for top-tier carriers on high-risk lanes, and 'eyes on pickup', where a local trucker sits at the shipper's dock and confirms the right driver and truck load the freight (aimed at high-value copper, electronics and pharma loads). Build the checklist with a trucking-defense attorney so it holds up as evidence.
why_now: The May 2026 Montgomery ruling created a brand-new legal duty and every broker general counsel is scrambling. Insurers are repricing broker liability. Fictitious-pickup and impersonation theft keeps growing (Verisk CargoNet counted 158 fictitious pickups in Q2 2026). Meanwhile English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement and the February 2026 non-domiciled CDL rule are churning the small-carrier population, so more unknown carriers are entering the market.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees of $175 to $350, with the trucker keeping about 45 to 55%. Annual diligence-program retainers of $25k to $100k for brokers that want a defined audit cadence. Insurer premium-credit revenue share. A recurring data subscription selling carrier physical-condition scores back to the wider broker market.
non_obvious_insight: Any 20-year driver can size up a carrier's yard in 90 seconds. Chameleon outfits have one shiny truck, no shop, mismatched trailers, cords showing on the steer tires, and drivers who can't name their dispatcher. Digital vetting checks paperwork; a jury after Montgomery will ask 'did anyone actually look?' The product isn't a tool, it's discoverable proof of reasonable care. Drivers are already within 30 miles of nearly any carrier and sit idle on 34-hour restarts and at detention, so the inspector supply is cheaper and more credible than any consultancy's.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 vetted current and retired drivers from CDL forums and trucker Facebook groups and pay them per audit. Pay a trucking-defense attorney $2k to $3k to co-design the checklist and co-brand a 'Montgomery diligence protocol'. Build the capture app as a PWA with forms, geotagged photos and an auto-generated PDF. Cold-email 40 mid-size broker GCs and compliance heads, offering 5 pilot audits at $99 on their riskiest tier-3 carriers. Target 3 paying brokers by day 30 and 100 audits by month 3.

title: Regulator-Grade Black Box for Collections Voice Agents
one_liner: A vendor-neutral audit layer that records, checks and attests every AI collections call so lenders can prove the bot behaved.
customer: Mid-size Indian NBFCs, microfinance institutions, digital lenders and collection BPOs running voice AI (Mahindra Finance alone runs about 10M AI calls across 12 languages). The voice-AI vendors selling to them are a channel partner.
problem: Regulators penalize the lender, not the software vendor, for harassment, off-hours calls (RBI allows recovery contact roughly 8am-7pm), third-party contact and false promises. A hallucinated 'your loan is waived' or a threatening tone is a compliance event. No human team can audit millions of calls in 12 languages. Household debt stress is rising (Indonesia paylater defaults, Brazil 82% household-debt indicator), so collection volume and scrutiny are both increasing.
solution: A third-party layer that ingests call audio or streams, runs in-language policy checks (hours, DND and consent status, forbidden phrases, promise-making, tone) and writes a hash-chained call ledger. Native-speaker reviewers sample 1-3% of flagged calls. Each month it issues a regulator-ready attestation pack with violation rates by vendor and script version. Lenders can gate scripts or vendors on the scores, and insurers of the vendors can use the same pack.
why_now: Indian voice-AI orchestration has exploded (Ringg, Bolna, Gnani, Blue Machines) and lenders now run millions of AI calls. ISO's gen-AI exclusions and Verisk's agentic exclusions are pushing carriers to demand evidence before covering AI conduct. Rising defaults in Indonesia and Brazil mean the same product exports.
revenue_model: Per-call-minute fee (roughly Rs 0.10-0.30) or annual attestation subscription of Rs 15-50 lakh per lender, plus a reseller margin through voice-AI vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The vendor can never be its own auditor, and the buyer's budget comes from penalty avoidance, not from a tech line. That makes this a compliance-assurance purchase like a statutory audit, which is stickier and higher-priced than a monitoring dashboard. Whoever becomes the accepted attestor also becomes the data source insurers price from.
first_30_days: Offer a free retrospective audit of 10,000 already-recorded calls to three NBFCs or collection BPOs. Build it on open ASR plus a rules library in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil, with two native reviewers. Deliver a violations report to the chief compliance officer, then convert to a monthly attestation contract.
